newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European body to defy call for fur ban.
newsitem.headline: European body to defy call for fur ban.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to defy calls by European Union environmental officials for a ban on fur imports aimed at forcing the United States, Canada and Russia to move in talks on trap standards, EU officials said Tuesday.

The commission is instead likely to agree to give the officials the text of a draft deal it negotiated on trapping standards, challenging them to reject it formally if they don't like it, said one senior commission official who asked not to be named.
Meetings earlier this week gave few clues to the outcome of Wednesday's full commission session, and most officials preferred to remain quiet on their commissioners' positions.
But several predicted a victory for European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan over his environmental counterpart, Ritt Bjerregaard.

Brittan's officials have argued against the ban, saying it risked sparking retaliatory action in the World Trade Organisation, while those working for Bjerregaard have said the commission should follow the environment ministers' instructions.
Those instructions, approved Dec. 9, were for the commission to take the steps needed as of Jan. 1 for the introduction of an import ban to take effect no later than March 31.
Ministers also asked the commission to reopen talks with the three countries "with a view to reaching a more satisfactory agreement" on trap standards negotiated by the commission, Canada and Russia.
The draft deal foresees standards for traps intended to kill or catch 18 species of wild animals, including muskrats, beavers, sable, lynx and wolves.

It would outlaw steel-jawed, leg-hold traps beginning four years after it took effect but would leave unclear the phase-out period for restraining traps, which it defined as those which neither kill captured animals nor inflict any of a list of injuries ranging from bone fracture, severe internal organ damage or limb amputation.
National and international animal welfare groups have already damned the draft standards as a "cynical political solution" to threats of WTO retaliation.
